title: Stand Firm in Faith: The Sign of Immanuel
summary: When the kings of Aram and Israel march against Jerusalem, King Ahaz and his people tremble. Isaiah meets Ahaz with his son Shear-jashub and tells him to be calm, for the plot will fail, but warns that if he does not stand firm in faith he will not stand at all. Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, so the Lord gives one anyway: the virgin will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, and before the child is old enough to choose between good and evil, the two threatening kings will be gone. But Assyria, the power Ahaz trusts, will devastate Judah itself.
story: Chapter 6 told of Isaiah's call to speak to a people who would not listen. Chapter 7 shows that commission in action, as Isaiah speaks to the king himself. This chapter begins a section (chapters 7 to 12) sometimes called the Book of Immanuel, which moves from Ahaz's unbelief to promises of a child and a king who will rule in justice. The house of David, to whom God promised an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7), is represented by a frightened king who would rather trust Assyria than God. The Immanuel sign stands at the center of that crisis, offering both reassurance and warning, and it sets up the promises of chapters 8, 9, and 11.
historical:
The setting is the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734 to 732 BC (the name comes from Syria, that is Aram, and Ephraim, another name for the northern kingdom of Israel). Rezin king of Aram, ruling from Damascus, and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel, ruling from Samaria, were organizing resistance to Assyria and tried to force Judah to join. When Ahaz refused, they invaded to replace him with a puppet king, the son of Tabeal (verse 6), who is otherwise unknown. Second Kings 16:5-9 and 2 Chronicles 28 describe the same events. Against Isaiah's counsel, Ahaz sent silver and gold from the temple to Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria and declared himself his servant (2 Kings 16:7-8).

Assyria responded quickly. Tiglath-pileser took Damascus in 732 BC and killed Rezin (2 Kings 16:9), and he stripped Israel of Galilee and Gilead (2 Kings 15:29). Pekah was assassinated, and within about ten years Samaria fell (722 BC). The sixty-five years of verse 8 is harder to explain; many connect it with Assyrian resettlement of foreign peoples in Samaria in the following decades (compare Ezra 4:2, which mentions the Assyrian king Esarhaddon, who reigned 681 to 669 BC), after which Ephraim no longer existed as a people.
cultural:
Isaiah meets Ahaz at the aqueduct of the upper pool (verse 3), probably because the king was inspecting Jerusalem's water supply in preparation for siege. Water was a city's lifeline in war. Isaiah brings his son, whose name, Shear-jashub, means a remnant will return, a walking message that carried both threat (only a remnant) and promise (a remnant will return). Names as signs were an established prophetic practice; Hosea's children bore similar names (Hosea 1).

In the ancient world, kings often sought signs before battle through omens and divination. The Lord offers Ahaz a sign of his choosing, anywhere from the depths to the heights, and Ahaz refuses with pious-sounding words about not testing the Lord (quoting the idea of Deuteronomy 6:16). The refusal masks a decision already made to trust Assyria. Curds and honey (verses 15 and 22) were simple foods from herds and wild bees; in a land where fields and vineyards had been abandoned (verses 23-25), they would be what survivors ate. Shaving the head, legs, and beard (verse 20) was a deep humiliation inflicted on captives and enemies (compare 2 Samuel 10:4).
literary: The chapter is narrative prose with embedded oracles. It falls into two encounters with Ahaz (verses 1-9 and 10-17), each built around a prophetic word, followed by four short oracles that each begin on that day (verses 18-25), describing Assyria's coming devastation. Verse 9 contains a famous wordplay on the Hebrew root aman, to be firm or to believe: roughly, if you do not firm up in faith, you will not be firmed up at all. The same root lies behind the word amen. The phrase house of David (verses 2 and 13) signals that the dynasty, not only Ahaz, is on trial. Many of the you forms in verses 13 and 14 are plural, addressing the royal house. The name Immanuel will return in 8:8 and 8:10, binding chapters 7 and 8 together.

outline.t: Isaiah meets Ahaz: stand firm in faith
Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign
Four oracles of the coming devastation

doctrines.note: Verse 9 is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements about faith: to believe God is to stand, and not to believe is to fall. Faith here is not a feeling but reliance on God's word in a real political crisis, rather than on human power.

The sign of Immanuel, God with us, is connected with the house of David and anticipates the royal child of 9:6-7 and the shoot of Jesse in 11:1. Christians read it as fulfilled in Jesus' birth, as Matthew does.

God controls the outcome: the plot of Aram and Israel will not stand, and Assyria, whom Ahaz hires as a savior, will come as God's razor. The powers of the world serve God's purposes even when they do not know it.

words.note: Almah, translated virgin in the BSB and many English Bibles, and young woman in others. It refers to a young woman of marriageable age and appears about seven times in the Hebrew Bible (for example Rebekah before marriage in Genesis 24:43 and Miriam as a girl in Exodus 2:8). The more specific Hebrew word for a virgin is betulah, though even that word sometimes needs a clarifying phrase. In the Old Testament, almah is never clearly used of a married woman, and the young women it describes would ordinarily be presumed virgins.

Immanuel, God with us, from im (with), anu (us), and El (God). The name appears here, in 8:8, and in the phrase of 8:10. It can be read as a statement of faith (God is with us) or as a description of the child. Matthew 1:23 translates it and applies it to Jesus.

Aman, to be firm, reliable, or to believe. In verse 9 it is used twice in different forms for a wordplay: if you will not believe, you will not be established. It is the root of amen and of the word for faithfulness. Faith, in this vocabulary, is leaning your weight on something firm.

Ot, sign. A sign in the Old Testament is something that confirms God's word, sometimes miraculous and sometimes ordinary (a name, a child, an event). Ahaz refuses to ask, but God gives a sign anyway, one that will confirm both his protection and his judgment.

christ: Matthew 1:22-23 quotes verse 14 from its Greek form: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”). For Matthew, Jesus' conception by the Holy Spirit and birth to Mary fulfills Isaiah's sign, and the name Immanuel sums up who Jesus is. Matthew's Gospel ends with the risen Jesus promising to be with his disciples always (Matthew 28:20), forming a frame around the whole book. Within Isaiah itself, the child of chapter 7 is linked to the land (8:8), to the royal child whose names include Mighty God (9:6-7), and to the shoot from Jesse's stump (11:1), so that the sign grows into a portrait larger than any child of Ahaz's day. The church confesses that in Jesus, God is truly with us, fully God and fully human.

hard.q: Does Isaiah 7:14 predict a virgin birth, and how should Matthew's use of it be understood?
hard.a:
The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age, and the Hebrew adjective translated will be with child can also mean is pregnant. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made by Jews in Egypt in the last centuries before Christ, rendered almah with parthenos, a word that usually means virgin, and Matthew quotes that form. In the second century AD, some later Jewish Greek translations used neanis, young woman, instead, and the debate between Justin Martyr and his Jewish dialogue partner Trypho shows the question was already contested.

Jewish interpreters have generally read the verse as a sign for Ahaz's own day: the young woman may be the king's wife, with the child as a royal heir such as Hezekiah (though the chronology of Hezekiah's birth makes that difficult), or the prophet's wife, with the child as one of Isaiah's sons (compare 8:3-4 and 8:18), or simply a young woman present at the time. Christian readings fall into three main groups. Some hold that the verse is a direct prediction of Jesus' virginal conception alone, noting the definite article (the almah), the emphasis on a sign from the Lord himself, and the exalted titles of the child in 9:6. Others hold a double or typological fulfillment: a child born in Ahaz's day served as the immediate sign, while the fuller meaning, signaled by the name God with us and the later promises of chapters 9 and 11, was realized in Jesus. Others stress that Matthew reads the whole Immanuel section as a messianic pattern and uses fulfillment in a broader sense, as he also does with Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15. On all Christian readings, the church's confession of Jesus' virginal conception rests on the Gospel accounts (Matthew 1 and Luke 1), which Matthew sees as answering to Isaiah's sign.

questions: Ahaz's refusal to ask for a sign sounded pious but hid a decision to trust Assyria. How can religious language sometimes cover unbelief?
Verse 9 says that faith is the only way to stand. What pressures in your life tempt you to trust something other than God for security?
What does it mean to you that one of the names given to Jesus is God with us?
